title: Boltz: building towards programmable molecular design
text: Table of ContentsThe team setting the standard in end-to-end molecular design and discoveryScaling open-source models into a platformBacking foundational AI with BoltzAndrew Hedin, Byron Deeter, Marla Jalbut, M.D., Sam Bondy & Grace DaiPublished on Nov 18, 2026Two years ago, a small team of researchers out of MIT’s CSAIL and Jameel Clinic released a suite of open-source models. Matching the performance of their closed-source counterparts like AlphaFold3, these models have now become part of the default toolset for early-stage drug discovery and are used by more than 100,000 scientists across thousands of biotechs, labs, and top-20 pharma companies.These models are just the beginning of a much bigger vision to make drug design a programmable problem. The feedback cycle of drug development has traditionally run through physical experimentation and trial-and-error, bounded by human reasoning. With AI-driven property prediction and design, scientific reasoning capabilities can drastically expand, allowing researchers to unlock previously undruggable targets and generate novel therapies at a fraction of the historical time and cost.Boltz is driving this paradigm shift with their foundation models for biology and chemistry, and Bessemer is excited to announce that we’re leading their $110M Series A.The team setting the standard in end-to-end molecular design and discoveryBoltz is a London-based AI research lab building foundation models for biomolecular modeling, small-molecule and protein design. The three co-founders were among the core developers of the open-source models that came out of Professor Regina Barzilay's lab. CEO Gabriele Corso won the Best Student Paper Award at the NeurIPS 2022 SBM workshop for DiffDock, one of the first models to treat molecular docking as a generative problem and predict how a small molecule binds to a protein. CTO Jeremy Wohlwend led Boltz-1 for structure prediction. Head of Research Saro Passaro built Boltz-2 for joint structure and affinity co-folding. And last but not least, Boltz founding scientist Hannes Stärk led the development of BoltzGen, which is now one of the most widely used models for generative protein design.What stood out to us from the start is how much scientists trusted the models and the team long before Boltz spun out of MIT. Their open-source models have over 5 million downloads, and every partnership Boltz has established to date began as inbound interest from computational chemists and biologists who were excited to share the model’s capabilities with the rest of their teams.Scaling open-source models into a platformSince launching in January, the pace of Boltz’s progress has been remarkable. In June, they launched BoltzMol-1, their small-molecule design model, which cuts the time to a validated hit from months to weeks and cost from hundreds of thousands of dollars to as low as $10,000. The team also launched BoltzProt-1, their protein design model, which has nearly triple the hit rate of BoltzGen, outperforms other leading models head-to-head, and produces designs that pass strict criteria around developability, demonstrating their comparability to real therapeutics in the clinic.From day one, Boltz has built the platform to make models accessible and easy-to-use for scientists. Beyond its open-source offerings, the entire model suite shares a single lineage, letting scientists move from a structure to a binding prediction to a designed molecule in one workflow. Additionally, the company’s Boltz API, hosted inference offerings, fine-tuning services, and integrations with agents like Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini allow scientists to run Boltz inside their existing and increasingly productive AI workbenches. This ecosystem of tools is currently deployed at a number of top-20 pharma companies including Pfizer, Takeda, GSK, and Bristol Myers Squibb, along with DSM Firmenich, one of the largest fragrance and ingredient companies in the world.Backing foundational AI with BoltzIn software, AI tools like Cursor and Claude Code have become the default for where code is written. We think a similar phenomenon will occur in preclinical R&D, where AI tools like Boltz will move a significant amount of screening and design work from the benchtop to the computer. We’re seeing this happen today, as computational leads have described Boltz as indispensable infrastructure they run thousands of daily predictions on. These anecdotes align closely with our thesis on how AI is reshaping drug discovery from early research through clinical trials, as well as how molecule identification and structure design sit in the high adoption/high value quadrant of our pharma ROI scorecard.As these models continue to improve, the ROI they deliver will accelerate, and with it the design of novel medicines and enhanced chemicals that foster healthier people and a healthier planet. We could not be more thrilled to partner with Gabriele, Jeremy, Saro, and the rest of the Boltz team, the people who pioneered this field, as they continue to build and innovate on the infrastructure for the next generation of scientific discovery.Learn more about Boltz or join their team.ContributorsAndrew HedinPartnerAndrew Hedin is a partner in Bessemer’s Boston office where he focuses on investments broadly across the healthcare ecosystem, including new biotech therapeutics as well as software and services sold to healthcare verticals.Prior to joining Bessemer in 2015, Andrew worked at F-Prime Capital, Fidelity’s healthcare-focused venture capital fund where he invested in early-stage biotech and digital health technologies, as well as Leerink Partners as an advisor to the biopharma industry.He earned an MBA with honors from The Wharton School, where he majored in health care management and finance, as well as a degree in biological basis of behavior from the University of Pennsylvania.Read more from AndrewByron DeeterPartnerByron Deeter is a leading investor in AI, Cloud, Frontier Technology, and the Business of Sports.
